What you can ask of the World Economic Outlook: its 44 indicators

Source: R/weo_indicators.R
weo_indicators.Rd

One row for each indicator in weo_full, with what it measures in plain words. This is where to look first when you have a question and do not know whether the data can answer it.

Usage

weo_indicators

Format

A tibble with 44 rows and 7 variables:

indicator

chr The IMF's code for the indicator, as in weo_full, such as NGDP_RPCH.

indicator_name

chr The indicator's full name, as the IMF writes it.

topic

chr What the indicator is about, one of seven topics, such as "Prices".

units

chr How to read the numbers, in plain words, such as "Percent of GDP".

description

chr What the indicator measures, in one line of plain language.

countries

int How many of the 197 countries report the indicator for at least one year.

weo_column

chr The indicator's column in weo, such as real_gdp_growth, for the twelve that have one. Missing (NA) for the other 32.

Source

International Monetary Fund, World Economic Outlook Database, October 2026, https://data.imf.org/en/datasets/IMF.RES:WEO. Built by data-raw/weo_indicators.R from weo_full and data-raw/source/weo_indicator_notes.csv.

Details

The indicators are grouped by topic: growth and size, living standards, prices, people and jobs, trade and payments, saving and investment, and government finances. countries says how many of the 197 countries report each one, because coverage differs: every country reports growth, and fewer than half report net debt.

Transformations

The codes, names and country counts come from weo_full. The topics, the plain-language units and the descriptions were written for this workshop: the units restate the IMF's own scale and unit, and the descriptions are the workshop's, not the IMF's. They are in data-raw/source/weo_indicator_notes.csv.

Vintage

The IMF's World Economic Outlook database of October 2026. This table is a frozen snapshot of that release: it does not change when the IMF publishes a new WEO or revises these numbers.

Credit

Print this line under every chart you make from these data:

Source: International Monetary Fund, World Economic Outlook Database, October 2026, https://data.imf.org/en/datasets/IMF.RES:WEO.

Examples

library(tidyverse) # load the tidyverse: dplyr, ggplot2, tidyr and more

# The topics, and how many indicators each has
weo_indicators |> # start with the indicators, and then
  count(topic)    # count the rows in each topic
#> # A tibble: 7 × 2
#>   topic                     n
#>   <chr>                 <int>
#> 1 Government finances      14
#> 2 Growth and size           8
#> 3 Living standards          6
#> 4 People and jobs           3
#> 5 Prices                    5
#> 6 Saving and investment     2
#> 7 Trade and payments        6

# What can I ask about prices?
weo_indicators |>                          # start with the indicators, and then
  filter(topic == "Prices") |>             # keep one topic, and then
  select(indicator, units, description)    # keep the columns to read
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   indicator units          description                                          
#>   <chr>     <chr>          <chr>                                                
#> 1 PCPIPCH   Percent change Inflation: how much consumer prices rose on average …
#> 2 PCPIEPCH  Percent change Inflation measured from the end of one year to the e…
#> 3 PCPI      Index          The level of consumer prices, averaged over the year.
#> 4 PCPIE     Index          The level of consumer prices at the end of the year. 
#> 5 NGDP_D    Index          The price level of everything in GDP. Its change is …

# Find an indicator by a word in its description
weo_indicators |>                                  # start with the indicators
  filter(str_detect(description, "living standards")) |> # search the text
  select(indicator, description)                   # keep the columns to read
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   indicator  description                                                        
#>   <chr>      <chr>                                                              
#> 1 PPPPC      GDP per person at purchasing power parity, which adjusts for price…
#> 2 NGDPRPPPPC GDP per person at purchasing power parity with inflation taken out…
